label: GPT-6 Astra
output:
Dear Kelechi,

You said if I was serious I should put it in writing. Please find enclosed one serious letter, delivered by Royal Mail to your actual house. You thought you were making a joke at my birthday. Unfortunately for you, I teach teenagers for a living. “I bet you won’t” is not an effective way to stop me doing something.

So here it is: I think you should consider teaching maths. Properly consider it. Not resign tomorrow, not throw your calculator into the road, not send your manager a dramatic email. I want you to come with me to the training partnership’s open evening in Lewisham on Thursday 19 November, at 6pm. Listen, ask questions, and see what you think.

You can finish reading before you start arguing. I’m assuming you’re on the train, so at least I have you trapped for a few stops.

We’ve been friends since Unilag. I remember you tutoring half our hostel in Moremi before exams, explaining something for the fourth time while the rest of us were wondering whether prayer could replace revision. You got an A in further maths, yes, but that’s not actually why I think you could teach. Plenty of people are good at maths and terrible at explaining it. They do two lines of working, say “obviously”, and leave everybody else behind.

You never did that. You could work out where somebody had got lost, go back there with them, and explain it without making them feel stupid. You were patient, and you made us laugh when we were tired and panicking. I don’t know whether you realised how much that helped.

And before you tell me that was years ago, let us discuss Christmas. My nephew. The fractions. The plates of jollof rice.

You were supposed to be enjoying yourself, but somehow you ended up moving portions around and explaining fractions to a child who had already decided he couldn’t do them. He still talks about it. You probably remember it as something you did between eating and sitting down again. He remembers understanding.

That’s what made me say it at my birthday. I wasn’t just suggesting a random escape route because you were complaining about the same spreadsheet again. Although, my brother, that spreadsheet has now attended enough of our gatherings. Nine years at the same firm, and lately when you talk about work, you sound tired before you’ve even got to the bad part.

I’m not saying quantity surveying doesn’t matter. It does, and you’ve spent years becoming good at it. But being good at a job isn’t a binding agreement to keep doing it forever. You’re allowed to want something else.

On your last birthday you said, “I just want to do something that matters before 40.” I remember because you were being serious for once, and I didn’t want to spoil it by pointing that out.

Teaching might be that something. I can’t promise it will be. But I think there’s enough here for you to go and find out.

Last month, a Year 11 boy I teach, Damola, finally got simultaneous equations after three weeks of struggling. He looked at his working and shouted, “Is that all??” The whole class clapped. As if I had personally been hiding the simplicity of the thing from him for three weeks.

I wish you’d heard him. He was delighted, but also slightly annoyed that something he’d been finding so difficult had suddenly become manageable. Those moments stay with you. You go home and remember the expression on a child’s face, and you’re already thinking about what to give them next.

Now, because you know me and would immediately distrust a letter consisting entirely of happy children and algebra, let me tell you the other side.

When I started in 2019, I cried in the car park twice during my first term. Twice. I’m putting that in writing too. You can keep this letter as evidence, but don’t become irritating about it.

Teaching is hard. You can prepare a lesson carefully and still have it go badly. Marking feels endless. Some days the behaviour is wahala, and you spend far more time than you wanted getting everyone settled enough to learn. There are afternoons when you’re exhausted and still have work to do, and being patient doesn’t come nearly as naturally as it did that morning.

Being good at explaining fractions to my nephew doesn’t mean you’ll walk into a room full of Year 9s and have everything under control. You’ll have to learn how to teach a whole class, how to manage behaviour, how to plan, and how to deal with the days when your plan isn’t working. You’ll be new at something again after nine years of knowing your job. I imagine that part will annoy you.

It did get better for me. I learned, I became more confident, and I stopped treating every difficult lesson as proof that I’d made a terrible mistake. But I’m not going to pretend the hard bits disappeared. I’d rather you heard this now than accused me later of recruiting you under false pretences.

The money needs a proper look too. The route I’m suggesting is salaried: you get paid while you train, it lasts one year, and it starts in September 2027. That doesn’t mean your finances will magically sort themselves out. There would be a pay drop in the first year, and you need actual figures before making any decision. Ask about the training salary, what happens afterwards, and how pay progresses.

There’s the pension to consider, and the school holidays, though please don’t imagine I spend every holiday lying down while untouched exercise books mark themselves. Still, those things count. So does enjoying more of what you do all week. You’re the quantity surveyor; I trust you to examine the numbers. I’m simply asking you not to reject the whole idea before you’ve seen them.

And you’re not too old. You’re 34, Kelechi. A woman in my department started at 41. You would be bringing experience of working, deadlines, and maths being used outside an exam paper. You wouldn’t be starting with nothing.

At our school in Peckham, with 1,100 kids, two Year 9 maths groups have had a supply teacher covering them since September. I’m not telling you that to make you feel responsible for fixing staffing. You have enough responsibilities already. But it makes me think about people like you who could be good at this and have never seriously considered it.

I can picture you doing it. Not because the children would all behave beautifully for you, or because being funny solves everything. They won’t, and it doesn’t. But you’re patient. You notice when somebody hasn’t understood. You can make a person laugh without making them the joke. Those are good things to bring into a classroom.

Applications for next September open soon. There’s time to investigate, but I know how easily “I’ll think about it” can become another year of telling me about the spreadsheet.

So: Thursday 19 November. Six o’clock. Lewisham. I’ll go with you.

We’ll listen and ask the awkward questions, especially about money and workload. You don’t have to sign anything or decide your future that evening. If you come out thinking it isn’t for you, fair enough. At least you’ll know more than you do now.

Abeg, give it one evening. I have already invested in a stamp.

Your friend,  
who was apparently serious at the birthday party
